title: Harness OS role manifest
description: Role-based operating layer for multi-agent harnesses. A project declares its agent roles and their permission grants once; hooks/harness-os-role-gate.sh enforces them at tool-call time. Presence of this manifest at <repo-root>/.claude/harness-os.json activates enforcement for the project. See skills/harness-designer/references/architecture.md.

harnessOsVersion.description: Manifest format version. The kernel hook refuses versions it does not know.

mainSessionRole.description: Role bound to the top-level session (tool calls carrying no agent_id). Omit to leave the main session ungoverned. Must name a key of `roles`.

unboundAgentPolicy.description: What the kernel does when a subagent's role cannot be resolved (mixed-role parallel dispatch on builds without parent_tool_use_id / per-child transcripts). deny = block with re-dispatch guidance; readonly = allow Read/Glob/Grep/TaskGet/TaskList, with reads held to the UNION of every role's read.allow (a caller the kernel cannot identify may see what some role may see, and nothing else); allow = ungoverned.

roleTagCorroboration.description: Whether a plain (nonce-free) <<harness-os-role: NAME>> tag on a subagent's transcript must be corroborated against the dispatches this kernel actually recorded. off (default) believes the tag on sight, which is how resolution rung 4b has always worked. auto refuses a tag naming a role that was never dispatched, but only when there are live dispatch records to check against — with none, there is nothing to corroborate and the tag stands. strict refuses any uncorroborated tag. Two reviewers argued off is the wrong default, and on the merits they are right: every other rung anchors identity to something the caller owns, while this one believes a string printed in a file. It stays the default because auto also refuses a tag-bound agent whose dispatch was never registered — a resumed session, a hand-placed tag — and that is a functional break an operator should choose. Recommended: auto for any manifest with a dispatcher.

ambientDispatchClaim.description: Whether an agent whose role cannot be resolved any other way may claim the single unclaimed dispatch currently in flight (resolution rung 5). OFF by default since round 29: every other rung answers 'this agent is role X' from something tied to the caller (its binding file, its own parent tool_use_id, its own transcript tag), while this one answers 'some single role is in flight, therefore you are it' — it never checks that the caller is that dispatch's child, and it persists the binding. A reviewer demonstrated an unrelated fresh agent claiming a judge that was legitimately in flight, and writing the ledger. Turn it on only on a host that supplies neither parent_tool_use_id nor per-child transcript tags, where it is the only signal available; with it off, such an agent is unbound and unboundAgentPolicy decides.

runtimeProfile.description: Tunes `harness-os run --role <r> -- <cmd>`, which executes a command under Node's permission model configured from that role's path scopes. This is the RUNTIME half of write-then-execute containment: the static screen (write.codeCapabilities) makes an escape expensive, the runtime profile makes the read actually fail. Two limits it cannot escape, both reported by --dry-run: Node takes path prefixes rather than globs, so the profile is a coarsening of the manifest and never narrower than it; and Node's directory grants are recursive with no deny-list, so a granted prefix exposes everything beneath it. Keep secrets out of any directory a role's scope covers.

extraRead.description: Absolute or project-relative paths the RUNNER itself needs to read (node_modules, the toolchain, /usr …). Declared here rather than hidden in the CLI so the widening is visible. Defaults to node_modules plus the usual system paths. A path that contains the project cancels every scope in the profile — --dry-run says so.

extraWrite.description: Paths the runner needs to write beyond the role's write scope (scratch/temp). Defaults to /tmp — change it if the project itself lives under /tmp, or the grant swallows the project.

allowWorker.description: Whether the profile permits worker threads. Most test runners need them. Set false to deny.

dispatchTtlSeconds.description: Freshness window for dispatch-registry entries used by the registry-claim binding step.

mcpPathArguments.description: Teaches the kernel which arguments of which MCP (or other non-core) tools name FILE PATHS, so those paths can be held to the calling role's read/write scope. Without this, MCP tools are gated by name only. Key: a shell-glob over the tool name (e.g. 'mcp__filesystem__write_file'). Value: which tool_input fields carry paths, split by the access they represent. Field names are dot-paths into tool_input (e.g. 'args.path'); a field whose value is an array is checked element-wise.

read.description: tool_input fields naming paths the tool READS — checked against the role's read scope.

write.description: tool_input fields naming paths the tool WRITES — checked against the role's write scope (a role with no write grants is denied outright).

commandGroups.description: Named groups of Bash command patterns (POSIX ERE, matched against each pipeline/&&/;-segment of the command). Roles reference groups by name in bash.groups.

roles.description: Role name → grants. Role names double as dispatch-description prefixes (`<role>:` or `<role>-<slug>:`).

description.description: One-line mandate. Quoted verbatim in deny messages, so write it as the sentence you want an over-reaching agent to read.

network.description: Which network destinations this role may reach. A command group is a regex over argv and a URL authority is a parser problem, so a pattern that pins a URL prefix is NOT a destination boundary: a reviewer pointed `^curl … http://localhost:4173` at `http://localhost:4173@example.com/` and curl connected to example.com. Declaring this scope has every URL authority in a Bash command parsed and checked. Entries are host or host:port — a bare host permits any port, a leading *. permits subdomains, and `*` permits anything. Opt-in, like write.codeImports: absent, only the userinfo rule applies (a URL whose visible prefix differs from its destination is always refused).

tools.description: Tool-name gate. Patterns are shell globs (e.g. mcp__github__*). deny beats allow; absent tools → all tools pass to the finer axes.

bash.description: Bash command gate. Effective allow set = union of the named commandGroups + inline allow patterns; every command segment (split on &&, ||, ;, |, &, newlines) must match one. The kernel additionally denies indirection constructs ($-expansion, backticks, process substitution, eval, xargs, shells/interpreter one-liners as commands, find -exec, cd, brace expansion) for every governed role, checks redirect/tee targets against the role's write scope, and holds file-naming tokens to the role's read scope. Absent bash with Bash tool allowed → any command (built-ins still apply).

env.description: Environment variable NAMES this role may set in front of a command. A leading NAME=value is stripped before every other axis runs, so the kernel refuses any name it cannot show to be inert — this list is how an operator names one deliberately. The screen used to enumerate the DANGEROUS names instead, and PATH was not among them: `PATH=/tmp/evil grep …` passed as data and the shell then resolved `grep` to an attacker binary, dissolving every axis at once.

permit.description: Named indirection constructs this role may use despite the kernel's built-in denies — the narrow alternative to `unrestricted`. Permitting one construct never waives the others, and the allow-set, deny patterns, redirect-scope and read-scope checks still apply. Prefer this over `unrestricted` whenever a role legitimately needs one construct (e.g. "var-expansion" for a role that uses "$HOME").

unrestricted.description: DANGEROUS. true disables the kernel's built-in bash denies AND the allow-set check for this role — raw shell, with only explicit deny patterns, redirect scope checks and read-token scoping still applied. Every bash guarantee the architecture doc makes stops holding for this role. Use only for a deliberately trusted role, never to silence a deny you don't understand.

read.description: Read-scope globs (repo-root-relative; ** crosses directories) for Read/Glob/Grep/NotebookRead. Absent read → unrestricted paths. This is the role's context diet.

write.description: Write-scope globs for Write/Edit/NotebookEdit. Absent write → NO writes (write is opt-in, read is opt-out).

codeCapabilities.description: Host capabilities this role may author into EXECUTABLE files (.js/.ts/.py/.sh/…). Code a role writes is code something will run — its own test command, CI, or another role — and at that moment the code holds its own permissions, so an unrestricted capability inside an authored file voids this role's read/write scopes. The kernel therefore denies fs / process / network / eval surfaces inside authored code unless named here. Grant the narrowest set the work truly needs (a framework-driven test needs none).

codeImports.description: Non-relative modules this role's authored code may import. An ALLOWLIST, because the set of packages that reach the filesystem is open: 'dotenv' reads .env, 'glob' and 'fs-extra' wrap fs, and no list of dangerous names can be finished — so the role declares what it DOES import and everything else is refused. Test code has a small, knowable import surface, which is what makes this practical. Scoped names and subpaths are normalised ('dotenv/config' matches 'dotenv'); relative imports are never checked here (they stay bound by the write scope). Absent, package imports pass — the tightening is opt-in so it cannot break existing manifests, and `validate` warns for any role that authors and runs code without either this or the `harness-os run` wrapper.

dispatch.description: Roles this role may spawn via the Agent tool. Present → dispatch descriptions must be role-prefixed and prompts must carry the <<harness-os-role: NAME>> binding tag. Absent with Agent allowed → unrestricted dispatch.

skills.description: Optional Skill-tool gate: shell-glob patterns over the invoked skill name.
